So for them to use something that I think our community has heard time and time again, but to reclaim it, it's just so cool.”</p><p>A six-week summer program organized by the nonprofit Project Unloaded recruits teens from the South and West sides of the city, many of whom have seen the toll of gun violence up close.</p><p>Luis Delgado, a member of the T.R.A.P. team, said he almost lost one of his relatives to gun violence several years back.</p><p>“Thank the Lord that they ended up surviving it, but it was such a scary moment,” the 17-year-old recalled. “We didn’t know if they were going to live or not, and that just sparked something in our family that we wanted to get guns away from the household.”</p><p>During the program, Delgado and other teens got a crash course in how to develop a social media campaign from scratch.</p><p>They met with advertising experts who helped them shape their ideas. They produced their own reels and skits. And they even developed prototypes of merchandise for their campaigns, from t-shirts to travel mugs and totebags.</p><p>Though the program was paid, Delgado said, “I could care less about the money. It was more about making an impact in my community.”</p><p>Delgado said he talked about the T.R.A.P. campaign with his friends, sharing the videos his team filmed and the gun violence facts they learned throughout the program. He was so convincing that he managed to get two of his friends to get rid of their guns.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fb0000" name="image-fb0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/976deef/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd4%2F58%2Fcdc817614c48bf41dad3befb89cc%2Fantiguncontest-260801-05.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/394289d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd4%2F58%2Fcdc817614c48bf41dad3befb89cc%2Fantiguncontest-260801-05.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/19dd5ce/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd4%2F58%2Fcdc817614c48bf41dad3befb89cc%2Fantiguncontest-260801-05.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Team Trap presents their social media campaign during the presentation and judging of social media campaigns for Project Unloaded at the offices Havas Chicago at 24 E. Washington St. in the Loop, Thursday, July 30, 2026. Teams of students have developed original social media campaigns, complete with graphics, video, and copy, to educate their peers about the risks of gun ownership and encourage them not to own or use guns. | Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/19dd5ce/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd4%2F58%2Fcdc817614c48bf41dad3befb89cc%2Fantiguncontest-260801-05.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/32024c9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd4%2F58%2Fcdc817614c48bf41dad3befb89cc%2Fantiguncontest-260801-05.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/19dd5ce/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd4%2F58%2Fcdc817614c48bf41dad3befb89cc%2Fantiguncontest-260801-05.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Team T.R.A.P. presents its campaign Thursday at the Project Unloaded event.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“All throughout the South and West [sides] of Chicago, people believe that having a gun makes you safer,” he said. “‘And I told them, ‘Let's be real about where we [are] at right now. Were the friends we lost to gun violence safer with a gun?’”</p><p>“It didn't just take me one day. It took a week, a week and a half to talk with them … to annoy them basically with the facts, statistics, and show them that you can let go of guns because no one's gonna judge you. By letting go of a gun, you are showing courage that a lot of people sometimes just don't have.”</p><p>Kamari Markiyah Brown, from Lawndale, said she was set on buying her own gun before she joined Project Unloaded.</p><p>“I felt unsafe, especially with what's happening to young Black teens like myself,” she said.</p><p>She changed her mind after she learned through the program that having a gun at home increases the risk of suicide.</p><p>“Now that I know that,” she said, "I do not want anything to do with a gun.”</p><p>Brown said the program has changed how she perceives her neighborhood and the world around her.</p><p>“I knew the world was unsafe, but I didn't realize it was to this extent,” she said. “But I also didn't realize how much effect I could have on my peers.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/06/05/scooter-escooters-lane-tech-safety-teenagers-crashes" target="_blank" >For Chicago teens, e-scooters are fun, convenient but sometimes dangerous, even deadly</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: How we photographed the aftermath of basketball coach Tim Bankston's shooting
entries.summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from Visual Journalist <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/candace-chambers" target="_blank" >Candace Dane Chambers</a>.</p><h3><b>What makes this photo important?</b></h3><p>Former South Side basketball star and current beloved high school coach Tim Bankston was found shot dead in an Auburn Gresham home on Wednesday morning. Bankston’s community impact spanned decades, first making waves as the Simeon Academy point guard who led the high school to a 1984 state championship. Bankston began coaching at Thornton Fractional North High School in 2002 and was inducted into the Illinois Basketball Coaches Hall of Fame just two short years later. On Wednesday, his influence was on full display as former teammates, players, family and friends poured into the street to mourn.</p><h3><b>How did you get this photo?</b></h3><p>I arrived to the scene later than my reporting colleague, Mike O'Brien, as I was coming from another assignment in Lansing, where a tornado devastated residents earlier this week. By the time I made it to Auburn Gresham, he had already conducted two interviews and walked away to write a quick brief to break the story. So I came in solo and tried to use context clues to figure out who may be Bankston's loved one's while also trying to be as respectful as possible of their grief. I hung to the sides and used my long lens to capture emotional moments like this one. I offered my condolences when appropriate, but ultimately tried to minimize my presence in an attempt to be minimally invasive.</p><h3><b>Technical details:</b></h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" entries.title: Heavy rains delay opening of doors at Lollapalooza on Day 3
entries.summary: <p>Gates opening for Lollapalooza Day 3 have been delayed until 2 p.m. due to heavy rains, organizers announced Saturday morning.</p><p>It wasn’t immediately clear what the delay would mean for the lineup; the first artists were scheduled to take the stage starting at 12 p.m. Chicago disco-funk artist Ric Wilson is slated to perform at 1:15 p.m.</p><p>Periods of widespread torrential rainfall are expected to amount 1-2 inches, according to the National Weather Service, with localized amounts over 2-3 inches. The weather service also issued a flood warning Saturday, which is in effect until 1 p.m.</p><p>Organizers encourage attendees to follow the festival’s social media accounts and the app for the latest updates.</p><p><i>This is a developing story; check back for updates. </i></p>
entries.author: Dorothy Hernandez

entries.title: Bears send fans home from training camp after lightning warning
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> sent fans home from Halas Hall minutes before the start of Saturday’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/07/31/bears-training-camp-report-practice-no-3-two-minute-drill-ben-johnson-caleb-williams-colston-loveland-kyle-long-nfl" target="_blank" >practice</a> because of the threat of lightning and decided to begin their practice indoors to the Walter Payton Center.</p><p>Coach Ben Johnson seemed fine with practicing in the rain. Despite storms that stretched overnight into the morning, the Bears kept the practice open to the public. That changed with the lightning warning. The team offered a discount in the team store to fans who had to leave.</p><p>About an hour before practice began, special teams coordinator Richard Hightower said he was looking forward to practicing in a "squall" later in the day.</p><p>"Embrace the opportunity to go out in the wet and rainy weather ... " he said "Because we get to work ball security. The returners get to work that. We get to see it. The snappers can snap the ball in this type of weather. We get to see if we can kick in it and we get to see, you know, who is ready to rock and roll no matter what the elements are because as you know we play in Soldier (Field) and everything is unpredictable."</p><p>The Bears planned to move practice back outside after beginning indoors. </p><p>Saturday was supposed to be the second of 10 open practices this summer. The Bears will practice in Cincinnati and Nashville in August before preseason games against the Bengals and Titans, respectively.</p><p>Saturday marked the Bears’ last practice of a four-day run. They’ll have Sunday off before returning to Halas Hall on Monday for their first padded practice of training camp. </p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Illinois Institute of Technology cuts 160 faculty and staff just before fall semester
entries.summary: <p>The Illinois Institute of Technology has laid off approximately 160 faculty and staff just before the start of the fall semester, a university spokesperson said in a written statement.</p><p>According to an email shared with WBEZ, the university’s president said Illinois Tech is facing research funding cuts and “severe restrictions on international students.”</p><p>“The university has no choice but to pursue targeted reductions to address these challenges and protect our mission as an opportunity engine for all,” Illinois Tech President Raj Echambadi wrote in an email to employees on Tuesday.</p><p>Illinois Tech, which has its main campus in Bronzeville and a law center downtown, is not the only university with these struggles. The Trump administration has significantly cut federal funding for university research and tightened regulations on foreign students.</p><p>The changes have discouraged and even disallowed international students from coming to the United States, which is hurting college finances. Foreign students typically pay higher tuition than domestic students.</p><p>The university reported that <a class="Link" href="https://www.iit.edu/oii/facts-and-reports" target="_blank" ><u>more than 40%</u></a> of students were from countries outside the U.S. in fall 2025. Six in 10 graduate students at the school were foreign.</p><p>Enrollment data posted on archives of Illinois Tech's website show a loss of approximately 1,200 international graduate students between the fall of 2024 and 2025 — a significant decline for a school that enrolled 7,500 students overall last year.</p><p>An Illinois Tech spokesperson did not detail how many faculty and staff have been laid off in each department. But several educators at the school said the cuts were deep and compounded by months of attrition following rumors of financial instability.</p><p>The university spokesperson said leaders recognize the changes “have a significant impact” on laid-off employees and are “committed to providing impacted colleagues with severance.”</p><p>“As always, we will continue to place students at the center of all that we do and to ensure educational excellence at Illinois Tech,” the spokesperson wrote in an email.</p><p>The university’s faculty senate issued a vote of no confidence in the president and provost on Monday, the day before faculty and staff began receiving layoff notices. In a letter to the university’s attorney shared with WBEZ, senate members acknowledged the campus is facing “extreme” financial difficulties but criticized how senior officials have handled them.</p><p>“The faculty do not trust the current senior administration to make the necessary decisions to navigate this transition in a way that meets our responsibilities to students and accreditors,” faculty members wrote in their no-confidence resolution. “The current senior administration’s slow, opaque, apparently uninformed and non-transparent addressing of the crisis has deepened and aggravated its scope.”</p><p>Multiple employees said campus leadership have yet to communicate with students about the layoffs. The fall semester starts for much of the campus on Aug. 17.</p><p>“Students are concerned that we're going to be closed in two years, three years,” said one staffer who asked to remain anonymous because they fear retaliation from university administration. “They're worried they're not going to get the courses that they need because we don't have the faculty to teach them.”</p><p><b><i>Correction:</i></b><i> This story was corrected to reflect that the quote about faculty senate members' concerns came from their resolution.</i></p><p><i>Lisa Kurian Philip covers higher education for WBEZ, in partnership with</i> <a class="Link" href="https://www.opencampusmedia.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Open Campus</i></a><i>.</i></p>

entries.title: Review: Charli xcx delivers jaw-dropping drama amid made-for-movies downpour
entries.summary: <p>Draped in black and hanging onto a microphone stand, Charli xcx listlessly sang “I think the dance floor is dead,” a vocal-fried message from her song “Rock Music” seemingly lost on the thousands of fans who headbanged, jumped and most definitely danced throughout the British pop superstar’s headlining set at Lollapalooza on Friday.</p><p>Helping her tear through her 23-song set was a three-piece rock ensemble, about 15 dancers and a made-for-the-movies downpour for peak dramatic effect.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" The musician said hardly a word between songs, choosing instead to let each bleed into the next.</p><p>And it was pure drama when Charli played 2020’s “pink diamond,” a heady hyperpop track from 2020 that ended with a torrential downpour before giving way to a brooding monologue from rock legend John Cale that’s featured on her song “House,” penned for this year’s “Wuthering Heights” movie adaptation. entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams must keep climbing no matter how it goes with offensive line this season
entries.summary: <p>For years, the Bears haven’t done enough to protect their young quarterbacks. Each of them, whether it was Mitch Trubisky, Justin Fields or now Caleb Williams, has been responsible for their own trajectory, but a little more time in the pocket would’ve helped.</p><p>You would think an organization so in love with the glory days of old-school football wouldn’t need a reminder that everything starts in the trenches, but Ben Johnson grabbed the Bears by their collective shirt collars when he arrived at Halas Hall last year and made sure they didn’t miss it.</p><p>The NFL’s best offensive lines are built with premium resources — expensive free agents and high draft picks — and it’s not a place to cut corners. Sure enough, once they spent big to bring in left guard Joe Thuney, right guard Jonah Jackson and center Drew Dalman, it made Williams’ life easier.</p><p>Some problems the Bears believed they’d solved, though, came unraveled when Dalman stunned them by retiring at 27 and Trapilo suffered a major knee injury against the Packers.</p><p>That means they’re undergoing yet another significant reset on the offensive line, where cohesion is key and can’t be microwaved.</p><p>“A big part of o-line play is all five of us need a gel,” right tackle Darnell Wright said. “That's a growing process. But it'll get better. It's gotten better.”</p><p>Going into his third season, Williams must progress and step into stardom regardless of what happens on the offensive line. The Bears are weighing whether to commit to a massive contract, and those don’t come with asterisks. They go to sure things.</p><p>Patrick Mahomes has made it work behind some shaky offensive lines, and Aaron Rodgers twice made the Pro Bowl despite taking 50 sacks in his early years. A quarterback isn’t special if he needs everything around him to be perfect.</p><p>It’s on Williams to take the next step in everything from footwork to decision making, and it’s certainly part of a franchise quarterback’s job to navigate and compensate for any potential roster deficiencies. But the sturdier the line is, the easier it’ll be for him to figure that out.</p><p>A faulty line was a decent-sized part of the pie chart for Williams’ mostly wasted rookie season, along coaching incompetence and his own shortfalls in throwing accuracy, indecisiveness and waiting too long for big plays to open up. That losing equation added up to a league-high 68 sacks.</p><p>The Bears rolled out a better formula last season: Williams was coached harder with no choice but to align with Johnson’s vision for the passing attack and the offensive line was dramatically better. Just 24 sacks trying it that way.</p><p>When Williams analyzed that reduction recently, he briefly mentioned having more trust in the offensive line last season, but stuck mostly to his accountability to avoid trouble with awareness before and after the snap.</p><p>The offensive line the Bears settled into late last season could’ve carried them through 2027 or beyond, and it was maddening to be readdressing it so soon after pouring money into the unit.</p><p>This time, however, they had fewer resources to throw at it as they explored options at left tackle and center. Their salary-cap situation was tight, which led to — on paper — shipping out more talent than they acquired, and by the time their first-round pick in the draft came up at No. 25 overall, the top six offensive tackles were gone.</p><p>They opted to pick up Dalman’s eventual replacement, Logan Jones, in the second round and roll with veteran Garrett Bradbury until he’s ready. Bradbury started on the Patriots’ Super Bowl team last season, is leading the line capably at the moment and almost certainly will be the starter.</p><p>“With Garrett, it really has been flawless so far,” tight end Cole Kmet said. “We haven’t had the pads on, but when you talk about the communication... things have been really clear and concise.”</p><p>The Bears still don’t know definitively whether left tackle needs a long-term solution because of Trapilo’s injury. They aren’t planning on him doing anything this season, but they’ve become increasingly optimistic over the last few months that it’s not a career-ender.</p><p>The idea of moving Wright to left tackle has been floated with Halas Hall ever since the Bears drafted him, but it’s never gone far. At this point, three seasons in and fresh off a second-team All-Pro selection, there’s almost no inclination to do it.</p><p>The Bears value right and left tackle similarly, and Wright likely will get a gaudy contract extension before the start of the season. He said recently he isn’t worried about that because, “I know I’ll be here for a long time,” and he’s correct.</p><p>So at left tackle, they’re counting on someone to emerge from a four-way competition among Braxton Jones, Theo Benedet, Jedrick Wills and Kiran Amegadjie. But what they’re really counting on is Johnson, with the help of offensive line coach Dan Roushar, engineering solutions through a combination of developing one of them into a viable option and scheming around any weak spot.</p><p>That’s one aspect in which Johnson set himself apart from predecessors Matt Eberflus and Matt Nagy last season. While those two seemed to get stuck when something went wrong, Johnson had Plan B, C and D at his fingertips.</p><p>The left tackle race isn’t as complicated as the Bears make it out to be. It’s Jones’ job to lose, just as it was a year ago, and the others will get chances to challenge. Benedet probably will end up as the backup swing tackle, and Wills and Amegadjie are fighting for roster spots.</p><p>The Bears are betting that this will be good enough, and while it’s never a good feeling to gamble at such an important position, everything about the offense feels like it’s in safe hands with Johnson.</p>

entries.title: Ahead of trade deadline, Sky's Tyler Marsh focused on team he has — minus Chloe Bibby
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> suddenly have a hole in their frontcourt.</p><p>Starting forward <b>Azurá Stevens</b> has been away from the team for the past week for personal reasons and missed Saturday's buzzer-beater win over the Aces. Coach <b>Tyler Marsh</b> did not offer a timeline for her return.</p><p>Meanwhile, the Lynx have poached one of her backups. Minnesota is signing development player <b>Chloe Bibby</b> to a standard contract. The Sky technically had the right to match the offer, but with their salary cap maxed out and all their standard contracts now guaranteed, they had almost no way to create space.</p><p>"It's bittersweet," Marsh said. "You're always happy for them. This is what development spots are for. Bibbs deserves to be in this league. We love and appreciate the things she's been able to do during her time here."</p><p>Bibby gave the Sky a useful wrinkle — more size and spacing — and contributed to two wins. She scored eight points with two assists off the bench in Thursday's win over the Sun and posted a career-high 14 points in a win over Seattle earlier this month.</p><p>The Sky can add another forward to their now-open development spot, but Marsh expects small lineups moving forward.</p><p>"Even with Bibbs playing last game, you saw a good amount of us playing small, with <b>DiJonai [Carrington]</b> in and <b>[Natasha Cloud]</b> in as well," he said.</p><p>This was a guard-heavy roster to begin with, and <b>Rickea Jackson</b>'s season-ending knee injury stretched the frontcourt even thinner.</p><p><b>Deadline day</b></p><p>The deadline to make trades is 2 p.m. Sunday, but Marsh's focus is on the team he has.</p><p>"We'll let [general manager] <b>Jeff [Pagliocca]</b> handle the trades and all that kind of stuff," he said. "I'm focused on who's in our locker room and what we have, and we're all confident in where we're at right now to be able to make a push."</p><p>The Sky still believe they can make the playoffs, and Saturday's clutch win buoyed that spirit.</p><p>But the odds remain stacked against them, and given the Mystics' recent success, the most likely scenario is still that the Sky send a lottery pick to Washington in exchange for a low first-rounder.</p><p>If Pagliocca could strike a deal to cancel the swap, would that relieve pressure on the season? Marsh basically said no.</p><p>"We're all in that same boat, feeling the pressure and weight of trying to catch a New York or Washington or whoever's in that eight spot," he said. "So it's not for me to worry about that swap. You take care of business and you don't have to worry about it."</p><p><b>No Diggins</b></p><p>Point guard <b>Skylar Diggins</b>, who has been out with a right knee injury since being moved to the bench, has not surfaced in any trade reports. Marsh did not have an updated timeline for her return, though he made a point to vouch for her attendance.</p><p>"Skylar is working with our medical team and her doctors as well," he said. "She's been in the facility every day practice-wise. Off days, game days. She's been around and been in the building. She's progressing. Not at a point where she's ready to come back. She's putting in the work diligently to get back as healthy as possible."</p>

entries.title: As Lollapalooza’s original fans grow up, attending with their offspring feels, well, perfectly fine
entries.summary: <p>“Is this interview about siblings or dating or something?”</p><p>The question, shouted at them by a group of passing festivalgoers, made 16-year-old Hunter Smith blush. His mother, Ellen Smith, couldn’t stop laughing.</p><p>The pair had traveled from Boise for their first Lollapalooza to see Swedish pop star Zara Larsson, Charli xcx, and other acts — a weekend of Some spend the weekend introducing toddlers to their first live concert and Porta Potty logistics. Others give their teenagers enough freedom to explore while staying close enough to offer advice.</p><p>For Beverly resident Beth Hagan, that preparation started long before her now 10-year-old daughter was old enough to understand the music itself.</p><p>“My parents frowned upon bringing her,” Hagan said. “They just picture it as more of a party atmosphere for older people.”</p><p>Aside from sharing the love of the Grant Park festival and dragging her to see The Smashing Pumpkins, Hagan said she’s able to teach her daughter how to navigate large crowds.</p><p>“Talking through things like what do we do if we get separated and things that I think are important — especially when you’re raised in a city,” she said.</p><h3>Glitter and lots of snacks </h3><p>Tucked inside Lollapalooza is Kidzapalooza. For more than two decades, the mini-festival geared toward kids has introduced young festivalgoers to live music through kid-friendly performances and hands-on activities.</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: THC-infused drinks generate a buzz at Lollapalooza
entries.summary: <p>Beyond the popular array of music at Lollapalooza, the other attraction creating quite the buzz this year is the introduction of THC-infused drinks.</p><p>For the first time on festival grounds, fans 21 and older can buy cans of local popular brand Señorita, margarita-inspired canned cocktails, containing 5 milligrams of hemp-derived THC in each 12-ounce can. The new offering is part of Lolla’s first-year partnership with Rolling Meadows-based drink manufacturer RYTHM Inc. And so far, fans are enjoying the option.</p><p>“I’ve never seen [THC drinks] at events like this,” said Jorge Gelan. He and friend Stefano Verdesoto, both 35, traveled from New York to attend the festival this year, specifically to enjoy the “very queer” lineup of music and were pleasantly surprised to find the new option menus at a comparable price point ($16) to alcoholic beverages.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-630000" name="image-630000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/92eaa88/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6983x3919+0+369/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F21%2F10%2F371c587b440e86e99f52986164bd%2Flollathc-260802-01.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9d77446/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6983x3919+0+369/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F21%2F10%2F371c587b440e86e99f52986164bd%2Flollathc-260802-01.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/99a9789/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6983x3919+0+369/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F21%2F10%2F371c587b440e86e99f52986164bd%2Flollathc-260802-01.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Customers buy Señorita THC drinks from a bar on Day 2 of Lollapalooza in Grant Park, Friday, July 31, 2026. For the first time on festival grounds this year, fans 21 and older are able to buy cans of local popular brand Señorita, margarita-inspired canned cocktails, containing 5 milligrams of hemp-derived THC in each 12-ounce can. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“To be able to access this kind of drink at a festival is crazy,” Gelan added. “I don’t drink alcohol, and I like THC drinks because I can still feel included in drink culture. And I like that it mellows me out and allows me to be more present.”</p><p>Gelan and others interviewed said the buzz is similar to the effects of an edible that doesn't bring on the typical hangover like alcohol. It's one of the reasons drinkers — especially millennials and Gen Z — have been switching over to THC beverages in recent years. According to a <a class="Link" href="https://www.crescentcanna.com/thc-beverage-survey/" target="_blank" ><u>2026 consumer study</u></a>, 76.6% of respondents had reduced their alcohol consumption in favor of THC drinks, including 21.1% who said they fully gave up traditional alcohol like beer and wine.</p><p>“We believe this is a major category in beverages going forward,” said Ben Kovler, chairman and CEO of Green Thumb Industries, which owns RYTHM Inc. The proof, he said, is in the partnerships the company has been launching as of late. Earlier this year, Señorita started popping up at the Near West Side stadium United Center, which was the first major U.S. arena to carry THC-infused drinks.</p><p><b></b> It was around the same time the drinks were unveiled at Salt Shed, 1357 N. Elston Ave. in West Town. The concert venue did so to capitalize on the growing NA movement that has been affecting bars and venues in dramatic ways as of late. Just <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/02/03/chicago-indie-venues-health-metro-ramova-salt-shed" target="_blank" ><u>one in four independent venues</u></a> in Chicago reported profitability in 2025, with many venue owners citing lower bar revenue as one of the issues. <b></b></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> </div><p>Kovler, a lifelong Chicagoan, said Señorita is now on the menu at more than 80 independent venues in Chicago, including the Riviera, Vic and Ramova theaters. “It’s good for the bar and good for the consumer,” he said. </p><p><b></b> Señorita is showing up beyond concerts and music events; the brand was also passing out (uninfused) samples of its lime jalapeno margarita, grapefruit paloma, mango margarita and ranch water at the health and wellness festival Faces of Fitness last week in River North. Kovler said the company takes its role in educating the public seriously and considers it part of the process of making THC drinks more mainstream. <b></b></p><p>But it’s the Lollapalooza partnership — and a previous deal with Sueños Music Festival in May — that gives his company an advantage, he said, even as cannabis products continue to face roadblocks with federal and local regulation. Sales data wasn’t available by press time, but Kovler said the team was expecting “thousands” of the cans to be sold during the weekend.</p><p>“Lolla shows us where the culture is, it’s far ahead of DC [and federal regulations]. And this gives us a huge stamp of credibility,” he added.</p><p>In June, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/06/15/illinois-hemp-delta-8-cannabis-regulation-bill" target="_blank" ><u>the state of Illinois passed legislation</u></a> that would regulate delta-8 and other intoxicating, hemp-derived products in the same manner as recreational marijuana. When the law takes effect in November, it could mean drinks like Señorita may only be available in dispensaries in the future. The Sun-Times reached out to Jillian C. Kaehler, a spokeswoman for Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, but did not immediately return a request for comment by press time.</p><p>The looming regulations may have played a role in its scarcity at Lollapalooza. Señorita drinks were difficult to find and only available at select GA, GA+ and VIP bars, though RYTHM Inc. did its best to market them, including investing in a flyover plane carrying a banner.</p><p>“I didn’t know where to find them. I was looking at all the alcohol tents and it wasn’t at any on the main strip — this is the first place I’ve seen it,” said Layla Contreras at a 21-and-over cocktail bar near Buckingham Fountain. The 25-year-old who lives near Midway Airport and is a regular consumer saw the drinks promoted on an ad on Instagram and was keen to find them this weekend.</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Bears CB Jaylon Johnson eyes next contract with Bears — or 'somewhere else'
entries.summary: <p>No one has been with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> longer than cornerback Jaylon Johnson.</p><p>That time may be coming to an end.</p><p>He planned it that way.</p><p>In May 2024, Johnson negotiated a four-year, $76 million deal that pays him $25 million — but with only a $9 million dead cap charge — in 2027. That makes him an attractive cut candidate after this season — and would allow him to reach free agency, where the market for cornerbacks has exploded over the past two-and-a-half years, just before his 28<sup>th</sup> birthday.</p><p>“I'm not a dummy,” Johnson said.</p><p>Johnson, then, is treating this year like the last one of his deal, even though it’s not.</p><p>“It's definitely a contract year for me,” he said. “Whether that's here, somewhere else, I've gotta put it on tape that I'm still a top guy in this league.”</p><p>That’s the most pressing issue. The Bears need Johnson to be reliable. Tyrique Stevenson, slated to start opposite him, has not been during his three-year career. Slot cornerback Kyler Gordon remains out with a calf injury after missing most of last season with the same malady.</p><p>Groin injuries limited Johnson to seven regular season games in 2025. When he returned for the stretch run after surgery, Johnson used numbing shots just to get through games. It wasn’t until the playoffs that he was able to play without being in pain.</p><p>It showed — Pro Football Focus graded him 68<sup>th</sup> out of 106 cornerbacks.</p><p>“I easily could have sat on my ass and not played and just watched it be what it was,” he said. “But for me I felt like what I had to give was enough to contribute to the team. Of course, it wasn't nowhere near who I could be. I feel like people know that.”</p><p>Time to recover helped. So did a newfound love of Pilates.</p><p>“I needed a full offseason to get my legs back under me, to get some scar tissue and things like that out,” he said.</p><p>No player in the Bears’ locker room has been more open about his contract status over the years than Johnson. He got his current deal months after he asked for a trade on the eve of the 2023 NFL deadline. Poles said he’d move him for a first- or high second-round pick, but didn’t get offered either. Another extension was on his mind as far back as last offseason, when he told “The Rich Eisen Show” he might have to revisit his deal. He hurt his groin training in Las Vegas shortly thereafter. Now Johnson is talking about his next deal again.</p><p>Contract status can make a difficult game even more complicated. Three years ago, the Bears talked to Darnell Mooney about a new deal during training camp. They couldn’t reach an agreement. Mooney, playing out the last year of his contract, posted what remains, to this day, the worst season of his career. The pressure wore on him.</p><p>Johnson has dealt with it well. He finished 2023 — the year of his 24-hour-long trade request — as PFF’s highest-graded cornerback.</p><p>“No, there ain’t no pressure,” he said. “I am who I am and I do what I do regardless of the circumstance. I’m just happy to be healthy.”</p><p>It’s the first time, really, that coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/07/31/bears-training-camp-ben-johnson-head-coach-confidence-year-2-ryan-poles-caleb-williams-nfl" target="_blank" >Ben Johnson</a> has seen him that way. </p><p>"He's highly motivated to garner the respect that, certainly, I had for him when I came into the building — because he felt like last year was a disappointment,” he said. “So, he wants to get back to being on the upper echelon of cover corners in this league. You kind of see that approach.”</p><p>Johnson wants the rest of the league to see it, too.</p>

entries.title: Noah Schultz delivers big bounce-back game, but Rays stymie White Sox' bats
entries.summary: <p>ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Noah Schultz needed that one.</p><p>After two stinkers coming out of the All-Star break put his rotation spot in jeopardy, the rookie left-hander delivered five innings of one-run ball after Jordan Hicks opened with a perfect first. But that one run was enough in the White Sox’ 1-0 loss to the Rays on Saturday.</p><p>“He was really good with the righties with the sinker glove-side and then used the cutter off of that,” manager Will Venable said. “So good job kind of dominating the inside part of the zone. He threw a ton of strikes.”</p><p>It was a promising development for Schultz, who allowed eight runs and 13 hits in seven innings over his previous two starts. Against the Rays, he retired nine of the first 10 batters he faced before running into trouble that he almost escaped in the fifth.</p><p>Jonny DeLuca led off with a single, stole second and reached third on a groundout to the right side. With two outs, Nick Fortes dropped a single into short left-center. Still, it was one of Schultz’s best showings of the year.</p><p>“I don’t know about ranking. I just know that it was a good day,” said Schultz, who threw 67 pitches, 47 for strikes. “I was pretty efficient, something that we were really trying to hammer in the last month or so. It shows that being efficient and getting ahead of guys makes a difference.”</p><p>The Sox’ best scoring chance also came in the fifth. Braden Montgomery singled and reached third on a single by Edgar Quero, who advanced to second on a throwing error. But Sam Antonacci lined out to right, the ball coming 105.1 mph off his bat.</p><p>Rays starter Drew Rasmussen stymied the Sox, striking out 10 in six innings. He allowed four hits and a walk.</p><p>“Just really good four-seam fastball with the lefties,” Venable said Rasmussen. “It was kind of cutting in on the lefties, and then we had some chase above the zone. And then really good job with the righties, too, with the fastball away. Just really good stuff.”</p><h3>Roch heads to Winston-Salem</h3><p>Shortstop Roch Cholowsky, whom the Sox chose with the No. 1 pick in the MLB Draft last month, will begin his professional career at High-A Winston-Salem on Tuesday.</p><p>“It’s the best place for him to get going,” Sox director of player development Paul Janish said. “If I’m being honest about Roch’s ability, he could go to pretty much any level. But I think it’s important to remember the trajectory, too. We’re just introducing him to the pro level. This is going to be the first time he has the opportunity to play six games in one week.</p><p>“If he was to go to Winston, play really well or struggle, we’re not going to put a ton of weight in it. That’s just the best place for him to get going.”</p><p>Infielder Landon Thome, the Sox’ pick at No. 36, will play at the Sox’ facility in Arizona with the rest of the players out of high school.</p><h3>Sox near bottom in ABS success</h3><p>The Sox ranked 28th in the majors in overall ABS challenge success rate in rankings released through Friday. Their hitters had a 46.8% rate, ranking 18th in the majors, but their catchers ranked 29th at 45.5%. On Saturday, though, Quero went 3-for-3 behind the plate.</p><p>“Working on the skill of challenging or selecting the pitch to challenge is tough,” Venable said. “There are things that we talk about as far as situations that you want to challenge, as well. Success rate is not necessarily the metric we internally are looking at for how we want to approach this.</p><p>“It’s really about, No. 1, you need to use these. The worst thing to do is not challenge a pitch that can really swing things. So for us, it’s being aggressive in the right spots, and then just doing everything we can to work on the skill of being accurate.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Bulls' Caleb Wilson will have a say in the race for Rookie of the Year
entries.summary: <p>The legendary Muhammad Ali was from the University of “It ain’t bragging if it’s true.”</p><p>Good to see all these years later that a new-school, 20-year-old like Caleb Wilson isn’t bashful about talking a few of those classes.</p><p>Since being selected No. 4 overall in a loaded 2026 draft, the North Carolina product hasn’t been shy about his intentions in Year 1 and how he plans to obtain those.</p><p>He not only declared in his introductory press conference back in June that he “expects to have Rookie of the Year, honestly,” but added, “I feel like the team is really good for me and how I envision to play.”</p><p>That’s key for a first-year player looking to do big things: Does he have the talent to put a Rookie of the Year campaign together, and maybe more importantly, is there roster opportunity for that campaign to be unleashed?</p><p>There are exceptions to that roster rule as Charlotte’s Kon Knueppel showed last season. The Duke product was the third option on a much-improved Hornets team but made a run at Rookie of the Year by rewriting NBA record books, becoming the first rook in league history to lead the Association in total three pointers.</p><p>Still, he finished second in the voting to Dallas’ Cooper Flagg.</p><p>What does that mean for Wilson and the ’26 draft class? Good news because Wilson has already displayed the want in becoming the top rookie, and considering this Bulls roster, will have the opening to do just that.</p><p></p><p><b>TOP ROOKIE OF THE YEAR CANDIDATES</b></p><p></p><p><b>Cameron Boozer – Memphis</b> – Vegas and the betting odds are mostly propping Boozer atop the class for Rookie of the Year and with good reason. With Ja Morant sent out in an offseason trade with Portland, the Grizzlies are scoring deprived. Boozer is a double-double falling out of bed and by the All-Star Break should be the best player on the roster, and by a lot.</p><p>Cedric Coward will take a jump in his sophomore campaign but shouldn’t take away from what Boozer does best and that’s why he is the leading candidate out of the gate.</p><p></p><p><b>Caleb Wilson – BULLS</b> – The three-point shooting Wilson displayed in Summer League was not an illusion. The shot is fundamentally sound and translates. Norman Powell’s presence will open up the floor for Wilson – and Matas Buzelis – but Wilson also displayed traits of a three, showing he can put the ball on the floor and go isolation.</p><p>But what will truly help Wilson chase down the ROY honor will be his above-the-rim game. Wilson is a highlight waiting to happen every time he touches the ball.</p><p></p><p><b>Darryn Peterson – Utah</b> – What to do, what to do? In high school, Peterson had the ball in his hands and dominated both with his scoring and play-making. In his one season at Kansas, he was off the ball – and off the court way too much – and his game was inconsistent.</p><p>If Utah gives him the keys to the car, Peterson has the potential to be both a dominant scorer and distributor with weapons around him.</p><p></p><p><b>BEST OF THE REST</b></p><p></p><p><b>AJ Dybantsa – Washington</b> – The overall No. 1 pick might be the most talented all-around player in the class but will have to share shots with veteran Anthony Davis and the ball-dominant Trae Young. What could help Dybantsa’s case is if the Wizards pull a Pistons and make a huge jump in the standings.</p><p></p><p><b>Darius Acuff Jr. – Sacramento</b> – The alpha guard will have the scoring numbers for the Kings and showed he can play-make at Arkansas. Zach LaVine and Domantas Sabonis will give Acuff some running mates, but the issue is he might be “Arius” Acuff by the end of the year because there’s no D.</p><p></p><p><b>Brayden Burries – Milwaukee</b> – The Bucks have a confusing roster in the wake of the Giannis Antetokounmpo blockbuster deal with Miami. A bunch of interesting parts with no real rutter to steer the ship. That’s where Burries fits in. The do-everything guard from Arizona could be the featured piece in helping Milwaukee move on from the Greek Freak.</p>

entries.title: 60 years after MLK protested in Marquette Park, marchers carry on his legacy
entries.summary: <p>Bernice King looked out into the crowd of rain ponchos and umbrellas Saturday morning, echoing the calls of her father, who stood in the same spot 60 years before.</p><p>The Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and other activists marched to Marquette Park in August 1966 to protest redlining and housing discrimination that spread in Chicago in the decades after droves of Black people moved north and settled in the city during the Great Migration. In Marquette Park that day, King and his associates were met with mobs of angry white people hurling rocks and Molotov cocktails.</p><p>This year, Bernice King joined Mayor Brandon Johnson, Chicago-born rapper Common and hundreds of marchers to commemorate the 60th anniversary of the march, reiterating that the fight for racial justice continues decades later.</p><p>Bernice King reminded the crowd of what her dad had dubbed the “triple evils” of poverty, racism and militarism.</p><p>“[Those] are still alive, still mutating, still menacing our communities,” she said. “They hide under new disguises, they show up in policies that punish the poor and systems that surveil the vulnerable, in structures that sacrifice humanity for profit.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Hundreds of marchers braved the drizzly morning, congregating at 63rd Street and Kedzie Boulevard before making their way south to the park to the tune of protest songs, chants and upbeat horns and drums. Some wore shirts reading “Sixty years later, we’re still marching,” while listening to speakers hype up the crowd with stories of Black resilience and calls to action.</p><p>Common performed with singer Mumu Fresh and a group of backup singers, bringing a gospel tone to the gathering as people cheered and raised their fists in the crowd.</p><p>In her remarks, Bernice King spoke of being a toddler when her family lived in Chicago in the 1960s, begging her parents to let her march with them. She addressed the crowd and implored them to keep addressing injustices, calling out President Donald Trump's administration and federal immigration enforcement for heightened arrests and entries.title: Sean Newcomb has seen buying, selling sides of trade deadline — where will White Sox land?
entries.summary: <p>ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Trades are being made all over Major League Baseball as the deadline at 5 p.m. Monday approaches. That includes the White Sox’ closest pursuers in the American League Central, the Guardians and Twins, who made deals in the last two days.</p><p>The first-place Sox have yet to join the fun and remained quiet on the trade front Saturday. Still, the players are keenly aware of the situation. Manager Will Venable made it a point to discuss the implications of the deadline last week at his monthly ‘‘State of the Sox’’ meeting.</p><p>Only a handful of Sox have been through a trade deadline with a team poised to make the playoffs. One of them is left-handed reliever Sean Newcomb, who was on a team that added and one that sold at the deadline.</p><p>It can’t be easy knowing the guy with the locker stall next to you might not be there after Monday. How has he handled it?</p><p>‘‘It’s what you make of it,’’ said Newcomb, a 10-year veteran. ‘‘I don’t think it’s anything that needs to affect us. We know the reality of it. Some teams end up doing nothing, some do a lot. There’s a wide range of things.’’</p><p>In 2021, Newcomb’s Braves acquired outfielders Joc Pederson, Eddie Rosario and Jorge Soler before the deadline and went on to win the World Series. Newcomb’s Athletics traded closer Mason Miller last season and sent pitchers Lucas Erceg and Paul Blackburn packing in 2024.</p><p>‘‘As far as the clubhouse goes, we’ve had guys talk about it,’’ Newcomb said. ‘‘There’s nothing you can really do about it.’’</p><p>Indeed, but players think about it, and those inside the Sox’ clubhouse have their opinions. Where does Newcomb stand?</p><p>‘‘I think everyone knows, even the front-office guys, if no moves are made, we’re just fine,’’ he said. ‘‘That’s the mindset that we have got to have. We just know from what we’ve done so far.’’</p><p>But . . .</p><p>‘‘Obviously, there’s always room for improvement,’’ Newcomb said. ‘‘I think every team can get better in some fashion.’’</p><p>Newcomb pointed to the fickleness of the trade deadline, too, specifically with the Red Sox. They got a jump on the trading frenzy by acquiring third baseman Curtis Mead from the Nationals just more than a week before the deadline. But in his second Red Sox at-bat, Mead was hit by a pitch and suffered a fractured left wrist. He might be back by the end of the season.</p><p>‘‘That instantly [put] them right back where they were,’’ Newcomb said. ‘‘That’s proof that there’s no need [for players] to put any thought into it, really. Just keep doing our thing here.’’</p><p>As Newcomb said, however, that ‘‘thing’’ still could use some improvement. Every team needs pitching. Only Sean Burke consistently has pitched deep into games, which these days is the sixth inning. And though the relievers have been lights-out lately, few have playoff experience. The Sox also aren’t getting nearly enough hitting from their catchers.</p><p>Those are needs general manager Chris Getz could fill if he chooses to. That decision will give the players something else to talk about in the clubhouse: Either the front office is going for it, or it isn’t. This much is certain: The players are.</p><p>‘‘This division is very winnable,’’ said designated hitter/outfielder Randal Grichuk, who has been through his share of trade deadlines in 13 seasons. ‘‘We think we’re just as talented as any other team in the division, and we think we have a chance to win it.</p><p>‘‘It has a chance to become the second seed, which is a better route to go, skipping the wild-card series. If you want to throw goals out there, that’s a goal. We’ve played ourselves into position to have that goal, and that’s what we’ve talked about as a team.’’</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-4a0005" name="list-4a0005"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="{pageCount=2530, borderColor=#dfdfdf, pageNumber=1, inverseColors=false, footerBgColor=#000000, bodyFont=font-3, showListNumbers=false, imagePositionHorizontal=null, rteBodyFont=font-3, headerBottomBorderColor=#111010, subTitle=null, stickyHeader=true, listTitleColor=#000000, tableCellBorderColor=#ccd1d5, items=[{type=Image, publishDate=August 01, 2026 04:35 PM, _styledTemplate=null, imageAlignment=null, title=Sean Newcomb has seen buying, selling sides of trade deadline — where will White Sox land?, url=https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/01/sean-newcomb-chicago-white-sox-mlb-trade-deadline-chris-getz-randal-grichuk-curtis-mead-red-sox, categoryUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox, description=[{items=[The first-place Sox have yet to join the fun and remained quiet on the trade front Saturday. entries.title: Sydney Taylor is the closer the Sky need
entries.summary: <p>Sometimes a basketball game comes down to one brutal reality: The other team has A’ja Wilson, and yours does not.</p><p>That appeared to be the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky’s</a> fate Saturday afternoon against the Aces. They erased a 10-point deficit to tie the game in the fourth quarter, only for Wilson to score the go-ahead basket with 3.2 seconds remaining.</p><p>But the Sky are developing a late-game superpower of their own.</p><p>Her name is Sydney Taylor.</p><p>Taylor’s late-game heroics have repeatedly put the Sky on the doorstep of wins they could not quite finish.</p><p>Before the All-Star break, Taylor scored a career-high 31 points in New York only for the Sky to crumble in the final minutes. Taylor was not going to let it happen again.</p><p>“That New York game has been on repeat for me since it happened,” Taylor said. “I was really due for one. I needed one really bad for me.”</p><p>Saturday's game was sloppy on both sides. Taylor missed open looks early, and the disappointment showed. But the great thing about Taylor is she doesn’t stop shooting — and she can heat up quickly.</p><p>She did in the fourth quarter. After a flurry of scoring from Taylor, a corner three-pointer finally sent Aces coach Becky Hammon cursing into a timeout. All of a sudden, the Sky were knocking on the door.</p><p>Taylor scored 13 points in the frame, but it took everyone for them to finally close out a game like this.</p><p>The return of guard DiJonai Carrington has made their defense much stingier down the stretch. Center Kamilla Cardoso trusted herself enough to hit one of her first jump shots of the season. Natasha Cloud converted a key three-point play.</p><p>“We constantly say, ‘Don’t let your bootyhole get tight at the end of the game,’” Cloud said. “We’ve been in so many of these late-game situations where we understand that at some point it’s going to tip in our favor.”</p><p>Taylor opened up at practice this week about wanting even more opportunities with the ball in her hands in clutch moments.</p><p>Marsh gave her two in the final 27 seconds.</p><p>With the score tied, he called for a clear out for Taylor to go one-on-one. She burst past Aces guard Jackie Young, but her floater bounced off the side of the backboard.</p><p>Taylor then watched Wilson respond from the bench after Marsh made an offense-defense substitution. She told herself that if she got back into the game, another opportunity would come.</p><p>It did.</p><p>With 3.2 seconds remaining, Taylor received a perfect screen from Elizabeth Williams, caught Cloud’s inbound pass and let a deep three-pointer fly.</p><p>“I don’t even know how close I was or how far I was,” Taylor said. “I just shot it. I’m glad my teammates had the confidence in me to take a shot like that against that team. That’s a big win for us.”</p><p>The moment was even sweeter given that Marsh had stolen the winning play from Hammon, his old friend and mentor.</p><p>“Our first year in 2022 we ran it in practice,” Marsh said. “Anybody that knows me knows I save everything from everywhere that I’ve been. I just pulled that one out, and luckily it worked.”</p><p>Lucky indeed. This five-game homestand is essentially do or die for a team still chasing a miracle playoff push.</p><p>Cloud, the Sky’s hype woman and heartbeat, still sees everything coming together.</p><p>“I know that the first half of our season was relatively ugly and painful,” Cloud said. “We kept staying the course, understanding that we’re losing these ones, but when it matters most, we’re going to have the experience.</p><p>“We have 11 games left [before the FIBA break]. We have two already checked off, and we’re taking it one game at a time. I’m just really proud of the resilience of this team to take all the adversity of the first half of the season so that when we do have games like this, it feels so much better because we’ve been through the [expletive] mud.”</p>
